newsitem.title: USA: ValuJet's Jordan expects strong return.
newsitem.headline: ValuJet's Jordan expects strong return.

text.p: ValuJet Inc President Lewis Jordan said on Thursday he expects business to come back strong, once the low-cost carrier resumes service on Monday.

He also discounted potential new threats from Delta Air Lines Inc's low-cost Delta Express, which begins service on October 1 and from Southwest Airlines Co, which has been taking steps to boost its presence east of the Mississippi River.

"From the feedback we have received from ValuJet customers and people who say they've never flown ValuJet before, but have followed our story and are supporters, I belive we're going to see a very strong comeback," he told reporters after being cheered at a news conference by jubilant employees.
"From the enthusiasm of our people and the customer service that they have said voluntarily they are excited to provide, we're going to see a strong return."
Jordan declined to discuss the company's financial forecasts, however, saying only that ValuJet executives are determined to run an efficient airline.
"We've done our homework. We have prepared for Game Day. Game Day is here. We're ready for the whistle to blow and we'll be out there doing a great job," he said.
Asked by one reporter how ValuJet planned to turn a profit on a $19 one-way introductory fare, Jordan responded: "We'll be making a lot more money than we've been making these past three months."

Tickets went on sale two hours after the airline received final government approval to return to the skies. Advertising was set to begin on radio on Friday and in newspapers on Sunday and on television on Monday.
"ValuJet will again return to its little airline niche and have a loyal customer base," he said.
"We know we will have to compete hard, we're planning to compete hard, we're prepared to compete hard and we think we'll do quite well."
The first flight was scheduled to leave Atlanta for Washington, D.C., at 12:30 p.m. EDT (1630 GMT) on Monday.
Jordan said that while the initial low capacity will keep unit costs high, he has few competitive worries about Delta or Southwest Airlines.

"Neither of them are serving Atlanta. Neither Delta (Express) nor Southwest Airlines have chosen to serve the Atlanta market. Our market research tells us that it's a very small percentage of our markets, even on a connecting basis," he said.

"We have been in very heavy competition, particularly with Delta Air Lines and USAir, almost from the start. They've been very very aggressive and we'd like to think we've been aggressive ourselves. I think will compete effectively."
